newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge blocks deportation of Nicaraguans.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge blocks deportation of Nicaraguans.

text.p: A U.S. judge, saying he had rarely seen such a "dramatic, heart-rending" danger of irreparable harm, granted a reprieve on Tuesday to thousands of Nicaraguan immigrants facing immediate deportation.
U.S. District Judge James Lawrence King issued a preliminary injunction to prevent the deportations at least until a trial early next year.

"With the drums of war beating an ever increasing cadence of death, destruction and misery across Central America during the 1980s, refugees, in the tens of thousands, fled their homelands," he wrote in his 67-page ruling.

"They came with the hope that a nation renowned throughout the civilised world for justice, fairness and respect for human rights would help them in their time of need," the federal judge wrote, rebuking the Immigration and Naturalisation Service for its treatment of the immigrants.

Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman, in Washington on a working visit, applauded King's ruling but urged the U.S. government to find a permanent solution to the problem of the status of hundreds of thousands of Central American refugees.

Aleman said at a news conference in the U.S. Congress that he would ask Attorney General Janet Reno later on Tuesday to revive an INS programme shielding Nicaraguans from deportation while their residency applications were being reviewed.
He said he would also ask Reno to overturn an immigration board of appeals' February decision that Nicaraguan asylum requests must meet a 1996 immigration law's tough provisions.
Aleman argued that his impoverished nation, like others in Central America, could not afford to receive the tens of thousands of people whom the United States might deport.

King's ruling, in which he set a date of Jan. 5, 1998, for the case to come to trial, followed several fearful months for the U.S. Nicaraguan community, which includes many former soldiers from the U.S.-backed Contra army and many parents whose young children are U.S. citizens.

Their fears were sparked by the tough new U.S. immigration law enacted last year. The legislation, which was applied retroactively to the Nicaraguans and other foreigners, revoked the right to seek suspension of deportation.

Ira Kurzban, a lawyer for the immigrants, said that meant as many as 500,000 people who had been living and paying taxes in the United States for years risked being summarily sent back to their homelands.

Thousands of Nicaraguans in Miami marched in the street to protest the new law. Others, leary of the INS, kept their children out of school, stayed away from church, shunned hospitals and moved from house to house.
A group of 41 Nicaraguans filed the class-action suit on which King ruled. It was directed against Reno, the INS and the Department of Justice.
After an earlier injunction expired on June 12, the INS promised there would be no mass deportations and said it would await King's Tuesday ruling.
But Nicaraguan officials said at least two Nicaraguans deported under the law arrived in Managua after being expelled from Miami within hours of the law's expiration.

King said on Tuesday INS officials had misinterpreted U.S. law when determining the status of Nicaraguans who were legal long-term residents. He also said Nicaraguans had paid fees to the INS and received special treatment not granted other immigrant groups before the government reversed itself and moved to kick them out of the United States.
"Seldom, if ever, has such a dramatic, heart-rending and powerfully persuasive case of irreparable harm to literally tens of thousands of human beings been presented to this federal court," he wrote.
In Washington INS spokesman Brian Jordan said the agency had not yet decided how it would respond. The INS maintained that King did not have the legal status to hear the case.
Nicaraguans in Miami responded jubilantly, holding an afternoon rally in the city's centre on a street where seven people ended a long hunger strike.
